solution_overview:
This problem examines the ownership of loyalty cards (Card X, Card Y, Card Z) among a retailer's customers. We are given the individual probabilities of owning each card, the probabilities of owning pairs of cards, and the probability of owning all three cards. Our task is to evaluate statements about the probabilities of a randomly selected customer holding various combinations of these cards.

Let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ be the events that a customer holds Card X, Card Y, and Card Z, respectively. We are provided with the following probabilities:

Individual card ownership probabilities:
$$P(X) = 0.52$$
$$P(Y) = 0.34$$
$$P(Z) = 0.41$$

Probabilities of holding exactly two specified cards:
$$P(X \cap Y) = 0.18$$
$$P(X \cap Z) = 0.22$$
$$P(Y \cap Z) = 0.15$$

Probability of holding all three cards:
$$P(X \cap Y \cap Z) = 0.09$$

To address the statements, it is helpful to calculate the probabilities of holding exactly one, two, or three cards. We define $P(E_k)$ as the probability that a customer holds exactly $k$ cards.

The probability of holding exactly three cards is directly given:
$$P(E_3) = P(X \cap Y \cap Z) = 0.09$$

The probabilities of holding exactly two specific cards (e.g., Card X and Card Y, but not Card Z) are found by subtracting the probability of holding all three cards from the pairwise intersection probabilities:
$$P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) = P(X \cap Y) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) = 0.18 - 0.09 = 0.09$$

$$P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) = P(X \cap Z) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) = 0.22 - 0.09 = 0.13$$

$$P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c) = P(Y \cap Z) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c) = 0.15 - 0.09 = 0.06$$

The probability of holding exactly two cards, $P(E_2)$, is the sum of these mutually exclusive probabilities:
$$P(E_2) = P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) + P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) + P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c)$$
$$P(E_2) = 0.09 + 0.13 + 0.06 = 0.28$$

To find the probabilities of holding exactly one specific card (e.g., only Card X, but neither Card Y nor Card Z), we subtract the probabilities of holding Card X with other combinations from $P(X)$:
$$P(X \cap Y^c \cap Z^c) = P(X) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) - P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(X \cap Y^c \cap Z^c) = 0.52 - 0.09 - 0.13 - 0.09 = 0.21$$

$$P(Y \cap X^c \cap Z^c) = P(Y) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) - P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(Y \cap X^c \cap Z^c) = 0.34 - 0.09 - 0.06 - 0.09 = 0.10$$

$$P(Z \cap X^c \cap Y^c) = P(Z) - P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) - P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c) - P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
$$P(Z \cap X^c \cap Y^c) = 0.41 - 0.13 - 0.06 - 0.09 = 0.13$$

The probability of holding exactly one card, $P(E_1)$, is the sum of these mutually exclusive probabilities:
$$P(E_1) = P(X \cap Y^c \cap Z^c) + P(Y \cap X^c \cap Z^c) + P(Z \cap X^c \cap Y^c)$$
$$P(E_1) = 0.21 + 0.10 + 0.13 = 0.44$$

The probability that a customer holds at least one card is the sum of the probabilities of holding exactly one, two, or three cards:
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = P(E_1) + P(E_2) + P(E_3)$$
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = 0.44 + 0.28 + 0.09 = 0.81$$

Finally, the probability of holding none of the cards, $P(E_0)$, is the complement of holding at least one card:
$$P(E_0) = 1 - P(X \cup Y \cup Z)$$
$$P(E_0) = 1 - 0.81 = 0.19$$
These calculated probabilities for exactly $k$ cards are $P(E_0)=0.19$, $P(E_1)=0.44$, $P(E_2)=0.28$, and $P(E_3)=0.09$. These values comprehensively describe the distribution of loyalty card ownership and will be used to assess the truth of the statements.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This statement asks for the probability that the customer holds at least one card. This is represented by the union of the three card events, $P(X \cup Y \cup Z)$. We can calculate this using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events:
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = P(X) + P(Y) + P(Z) - (P(X \cap Y) + P(X \cap Z) + P(Y \cap Z)) + P(X \cap Y \cap Z)$$
Substituting the given probabilities into this formula:
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = 0.52 + 0.34 + 0.41 - (0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15) + 0.09$$
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = 1.27 - 0.55 + 0.09$$
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = 0.72 + 0.09$$
$$P(X \cup Y \cup Z) = 0.81$$
This means there is an $81\%$ probability that a customer holds at least one card. The claim states this probability exceeds $79\%$. Since $81\% > 79\%$, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The statement concerns the probability that a customer holds exactly one card, which we denoted as $P(E_1)$. As calculated in the solution overview, this probability is the sum of the probabilities of holding only Card X, only Card Y, or only Card Z.
$$P(E_1) = P(X \cap Y^c \cap Z^c) + P(Y \cap X^c \cap Z^c) + P(Z \cap X^c \cap Y^c)$$
$$P(E_1) = 0.21 + 0.10 + 0.13$$
$$P(E_1) = 0.44$$
This result indicates a $44\%$ probability of holding exactly one card. The claim states this probability is above $42\%$. Since $44\% > 42\%$, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

This statement asks for the probability that the customer holds exactly two cards, represented as $P(E_2)$. In the solution overview, this was calculated by summing the probabilities of holding exactly two specific cards:
$$P(E_2) = P(X \cap Y \cap Z^c) + P(X \cap Z \cap Y^c) + P(Y \cap Z \cap X^c)$$
$$P(E_2) = 0.09 + 0.13 + 0.06$$
$$P(E_2) = 0.28$$
This means there is a $28\%$ probability of holding exactly two cards. The claim states this probability is at least $26\%$. Since $28\% \ge 26\%$, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The probability that the customer holds none of the three cards is the complement of holding at least one card. This can be expressed as $P(E_0)$, or $1 - P(X \cup Y \cup Z)$. Using the value of $P(X \cup Y \cup Z)$ derived in the overview:
$$P(E_0) = 1 - P(X \cup Y \cup Z)$$
$$P(E_0) = 1 - 0.81$$
$$P(E_0) = 0.19$$
There is a $19\%$ probability that a customer holds none of the cards. The claim states this probability is under $21\%$. Since $19\% < 21\%$, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

This statement asks for the probability that the customer holds at least two cards. This event includes customers who hold exactly two cards and customers who hold exactly three cards. Therefore, this probability is the sum $P(E_2) + P(E_3)$. We use the values calculated in the solution overview:
$$P(\text{at least two cards}) = P(E_2) + P(E_3)$$
$$P(\text{at least two cards}) = 0.28 + 0.09$$
$$P(\text{at least two cards}) = 0.37$$
This indicates a $37\%$ probability of a customer holding at least two cards. The claim states this probability exceeds $35\%$. Since $37\% > 35\%$, the statement is True.
